plain: The Robertson Panel, a group of scientists the CIA called together in January 1953 to review UFO reports, set out in papers kept secret at the time that the explicit aim of Project Blue Book, the Air Force's UFO study, was to throw the public off and to downplay, suppress and explain away sightings. Michels tells this himself, elsewhere giving fear of mass hysteria as the reason, crediting the physicist Hal Puthoff, and saying the panel's leader, the physicist Howard P. Robertson, created Blue Book's mandate; if true, the public study was built to mislead. The panel's report, written by the CIA's Office of Scientific Intelligence and dated 16 February 1953, does recommend a "debunking" aim to reduce public interest in "flying saucers" and lists the public's openness "to mass hysteria" among the dangers, but it states no motive of Blue Book's own, and Blue Book was already running when the panel met.

discussion.by: Report of Meetings of Scientific Advisory Panel on Unidentified Flying Objects (Robertson Panel), 14-18 January 1953
discussion.text: The tellers do not say which of the panel's papers they mean; in the minutes and the report read here the panel recommends a "debunking" aim that "would result in reduction in public interest in 'flying saucers'", names among the dangers the "Subjectivity of public to mass hysteria", and lists among the evidence it was shown the "ATIC Status and Progress Reports of Project GRUDGE and Project BLUE BOOK", so Blue Book was already running when the panel met. That the aim the panel set out was Blue Book's own motive, or that the panel created Blue Book's mandate, is the tellers' step, which the report neither states nor excludes.
